title: Perry v. Sindermann (1972)
summary: An unwritten tenure understanding could create a protected employment interest, and lack of tenure did not defeat a separate First Amendment retaliation claim.
notes: Stewart wrote for the Court (Odessa Junior College, Texas); Burger concurred, Brennan (with Douglas) and Marshall each concurred in part and dissented in part, and Powell took no part; the opinion is the companion to Board of Regents v. Roth, decided the same day.

sections.Parties: Robert Sindermann, a government and social-science professor at Odessa Junior College, sued members of the Board of Regents and the college president after they declined to renew his contract.
sections.Material Facts: Sindermann had taught in the Texas state-college system for ten years and at Odessa for four successive one-year terms. As president of a teachers association, he testified before the legislature and publicly opposed the Regents on college policy. The Regents refused renewal and issued allegations of insubordination. Sindermann alleged that an official faculty guide, statewide guidelines, and institutional practice created de facto tenure despite the absence of a formal system. Officials denied retaliation and asserted that no hearing was owed.
sections.Procedural History: The district court entered summary judgment against Sindermann. The court of appeals remanded to examine the disputed reason for nonrenewal and the claimed expectation of continued employment. The Supreme Court affirmed the remand while rejecting the idea that a merely subjective expectation sufficed. Powell did not participate; the excerpt identifies but omits separate opinions.
sections.Issue: Does the lack of a written contractual or formal tenure right defeat a free-speech retaliation claim or necessarily foreclose a protected property interest requiring procedural due process?
sections.Holding: No on both questions. Sindermann was entitled to litigate whether protected speech caused nonrenewal and to try to prove an objectively legitimate entitlement arising from rules or mutually explicit understandings. The Court did not find tenure established or order automatic reinstatement.
sections.Reasoning:
Government may deny a discretionary benefit for many reasons but cannot use denial to penalize constitutionally protected speech. The disputed motivation therefore precluded summary judgment independently of any property claim. For procedural due process, formal tenure was relevant but not conclusive. Contract principles recognize understandings implied from words, conduct, surrounding circumstances, and established usage; similar evidence could show an institutional commitment to continued employment absent sufficient cause. The quoted faculty-guide provision and systemwide guidance warranted factual examination.

The Court insisted that a subjective expectancy be distinguished from a binding understanding. If Sindermann proved the latter, he would obtain a hearing at which officials gave grounds and he could contest their sufficiency. That hearing right would still leave the substantive employment outcome to lawful decision. The case thus complements Roth’s threshold rule while illustrating a possible source of entitlement beyond an express contract term.

topics.lrs-o-new-property: A protected employment interest may arise from mutually explicit understandings and institutional practice even without formal tenure language.
topics.lrs-o-due-process-framework: Perry, with Roth, supplies the first step of the procedural due process inquiry: whether a protected property interest exists.
